## Overview

The tomato leafminer *Tuta absoluta* left South America for Spain in 2006,
crossed Africa within a decade, and was first found in Asia, in Turkey, in
2009. By 2018 it was in India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Central Asia and probably
Myanmar. Could it have spread that fast by flying? @Guimapi2020 asked with the
cellular automaton that @Guimapi2016 had built for Africa:

- the land is cut into cells, and time into months;
- a cell next to the invasion becomes **invaded** in a month whose mean
  temperature is at least 22 °C and mean relative humidity at least 55%, and
  **exposed** otherwise: the moth may cross it but cannot establish;
- an exposed cell becomes invaded in a later suitable month;
- exposed and invaded cells both carry the invasion on.

Their answer was no: flight alone would take about 20–25 years to reach
Southeast Asia, so the pest must have travelled with traded tomatoes and
people.

This implementation is an **adaptation**. The authors' code and data are not
published, so the climate is the CRU CL 2.0 climatology [@New2002] on cells of
1/3 degree, bundled with the package, and the reach of a month is set from the
timing of the source's maps rather than from its text, as explained below.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
```

## The climate

The bundled climate holds the monthly mean temperature and relative humidity
of each land cell of Asia. A cell can be invaded only in a month that meets
both thresholds. Much of Asia never does: the north is too cold, and the
deserts and steppes of the west and the interior are too dry in the months
that are warm enough.

```{julia}
c = tuta_climate()
months = dropdims(sum((c.temperature .>= 22) .& (c.humidity .>= 55); dims=3); dims=3)
suitable = [c.land[I] ? Float64(months[I]) : NaN for I in CartesianIndices(c.land)]
lats = reverse(c.lat)                    # rows run from the north; plots want rising latitude
northup(M) = reverse(M; dims=1)
heatmap(c.lon, lats, northup(suitable); c=cgrad(:YlGn, 13; categorical=true), clims=(-0.5, 12.5),
        aspect_ratio=1, xlims=(26, 180), ylims=(-11, 78), xlabel="longitude (° E)",
        ylabel="latitude (° N)", colorbar_title="suitable months", size=(850, 480),
        left_margin=3Plots.mm, bottom_margin=3Plots.mm)
```

## The invasion

The run starts in January from İzmir, near the first record in Turkey, and
lasts 25 years. Each cell records the month in which it was first reached and
the month in which it was invaded, so one run gives the maps of every year.

```{julia}
prob = problem(:tuta_absoluta_asia)
u = solve(prob; save_everystep=false).u[end]
function snapshot(u, year)
    m = 12 * year
    return [!u.land[I] ? NaN :
            0 <= u.invaded[I] <= m ? 2.0 : 0 <= u.reached[I] <= m ? 1.0 : 0.0
            for I in CartesianIndices(u.land)]
end
colours = cgrad([:forestgreen, :pink, :red], 3; categorical=true)
plot([heatmap(c.lon, lats, northup(snapshot(u, y)); c=colours, clims=(-0.5, 2.5), colorbar=false,
              aspect_ratio=1, xlims=(26, 180), ylims=(-11, 78), title="year $y",
              titlefontsize=9, ticks=false)
      for y in (1, 4, 8, 12, 15, 17, 19, 21, 25)]...; layout=(3, 3), size=(900, 620))
```

Green cells are susceptible, pink exposed and red invaded. As in the source's
Fig. 2, the invasion crosses Anatolia in its first four years and the Levant,
Iraq and Arabia by its eighth, establishing only in the south-west of Arabia;
it crosses Iran and Central Asia as exposed land, reaches the Indian
subcontinent after 12–15 years and Indochina, southern China and the Malay
peninsula after 17–21. Korea is reached overland only in the last months;
Taiwan, the Philippines and Japan are never reached, as the sea is too wide
to cross. The source's maps colour every cell
the invasion has reached, exposed or invaded, in red. They leave northern
Asia, Mongolia and Tibet untouched, where here the invasion crosses them as
exposed land; the deviations below explain why.

## The timing against the records

```{julia}
places = [("India", 2015, 28.6, 77.2), ("Nepal", 2016, 27.7, 85.3),
          ("Bangladesh", 2016, 23.8, 90.4), ("Kyrgyzstan", 2017, 42.9, 74.6),
          ("Tajikistan", 2018, 38.6, 68.8), ("Myanmar", 2018, 16.8, 96.2),
          ("Thailand", nothing, 13.8, 100.5), ("Vietnam", nothing, 21.0, 105.8),
          ("southern China", nothing, 23.1, 113.3), ("Malaysia", nothing, 3.1, 101.7),
          ("Taiwan", nothing, 23.7, 121.0), ("Philippines", nothing, 14.6, 121.0)]
yrs(x) = x === nothing ? missing : round(x; digits=1)
[(; place, recorded=year === nothing ? missing : year - 2009,
  reached=yrs(tuta_arrival(u, lat, lon).reached),
  invaded=yrs(tuta_arrival(u, lat, lon).invaded))
 for (place, year, lat, lon) in places]
```

Years after 2009 at which each place was recorded and at which the
simulation first reaches and invades it (at a city: Delhi, Kathmandu, Dhaka,
Bishkek, Dushanbe, Yangon, Bangkok, Hanoi, Guangzhou, Kuala Lumpur, central
Taiwan, Manila). Flight alone is about twice as slow as the pest was: it
reaches India in 12.6 years against 6, and Myanmar in 17.5 against 9, as the
source concluded. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, where the pest was found, are
reached but never invaded here: they are too dry in their warm months.

## How far the moth flies in a month

The source's text gives the moth's flight as 100 km a month, through a Moore
neighbourhood of radius 100 km. That is the reach of its Africa model
[@Guimapi2016], whose 25 km cells and 100 km neighbourhood carried the
invasion from Spain to Kenya in seven years. In Asia, a reach of about 100 km
(three cells here) is far faster than the source's maps:

```{julia}
fast = solve(problem(:tuta_absoluta_asia; radius=3); save_everystep=false).u[end]
[(; place, radius_1=yrs(tuta_arrival(u, lat, lon).reached),
  radius_3=yrs(tuta_arrival(fast, lat, lon).reached))
 for (place, _, lat, lon) in places]
```

With a reach of about 100 km the invasion is in India after four years and in
Indochina after six, and it crosses to Taiwan, the Philippines and Japan,
where the source finds no risk of natural spread. The source's maps match a
reach of one cell a month: one of its 25 km cells, or one cell of 1/3 degree
(about 37 km) here.

## Deviations from the source

```{julia}
foreach(d -> println("- ", d), model_info(:tuta_absoluta_asia).deviations)
```
